weeks.title: Power supply budget — parts, headroom, and the smallest adequate unit

lesson.title: Power supply budget — parts, headroom, and the smallest adequate unit
lesson.body_md: Work order ISH-4101: a donated tower is getting a graphics card so a youth club can edit video, and the old 450 W power supply is suspect. Start with a parts list and each part's rated draw from its spec sheet, not from a forum guess. The processor is rated 125 W, the card 200 W, the motherboard about 50, two memory sticks about 10 together, the SSD about 8, and the fans about 12, for 405 W. A supply running near its limit gets hot, loud, and less efficient, and real loads spike above their averages, so the bench adds a quarter on top: 405 × 1.25 is 506.25 W. The smallest catalogue unit that covers it is 550 W, so the 450 W supply goes in the parts bin. Bigger is not automatically better, since a 1,000 W unit idling at 60 W wastes money and often efficiency. Check that the new supply has the right connectors for the card, and never open a supply's case; the capacitors inside can hold a dangerous charge long after it is unplugged.
lesson.worked_example: CPU 125 + GPU 200 + board 50 + RAM 10 + SSD 8 + fans 12 = 405 W × 1.25 = 506.25 W → 550 W unit

weeks.title: Memory channels — the slots you choose set the bandwidth

lesson.title: Memory channels — the slots you choose set the bandwidth
lesson.body_md: ISH-4202 is a slow machine that has two good memory sticks in it. Desktop boards usually have two memory channels, labelled A and B, each a separate 64-bit path to the processor. Each transfer moves eight bytes per channel, so peak bandwidth in gigabytes per second is the transfer rate in megatransfers per second times eight times the number of channels, divided by a thousand. DDR4-3200 in one channel gives 25.6 GB/s; spread across both channels it gives 51.2. The previous volunteer pushed both sticks into A1 and A2, which sit on the same channel, so the machine runs single-channel and integrated graphics, which borrow system memory, crawl. Moving one stick to B2 doubles the path without buying anything. The board manual names the preferred slots, often A2 and B2 for two sticks, and the firmware setup screen confirms the mode after a reboot. Handle sticks by the edges, match the notch to the key in the slot, and press until both latches click; a half-seated stick is a classic cause of beeps and no display.
lesson.worked_example: DDR4-3200 in A2 + B2 → 2 channels → 3200 × 8 × 2 / 1000 = 51.2 GB/s; in A1 + A2 → 1 channel → 25.6 GB/s

weeks.title: RAID — usable space, tolerated failures, and why it is not a backup

lesson.title: RAID — usable space, tolerated failures, and why it is not a backup
lesson.body_md: ISH-4303 is a NO_AI week; build the table by hand. A community centre wants its donated four-bay storage box set up for shared files, with four 4 TB disks. RAID combines disks into one volume with different trade-offs. RAID 0 stripes data across all four for 16 TB and speed, but any single failure loses everything. RAID 1 mirrors the same data on every disk: only 4 TB usable, yet three disks can die. RAID 5 spreads one disk's worth of parity, leaving 12 TB and surviving one failure. RAID 6 uses two disks' worth of parity for 8 TB and survives any two. RAID 10 mirrors pairs and stripes across them, also 8 TB; it is guaranteed to survive one failure and survives a second only if it hits the other pair, so the honest table says one. With large disks, rebuilding after a failure takes many hours and stresses the survivors, which is why RAID 6 suits this box better than RAID 5. Most important: RAID protects against a disk dying, not against deletion, ransomware, or fire, because those damage every copy at once. The centre still needs the 3-2-1 backup plan.
lesson.worked_example: four 4 TB disks: RAID 0 16 TB/0, RAID 1 4 TB/3, RAID 5 12 TB/1, RAID 6 8 TB/2, RAID 10 8 TB/1 guaranteed

weeks.title: MBR or GPT — the two-terabyte ceiling and UEFI boot

lesson.title: MBR or GPT — the two-terabyte ceiling and UEFI boot
lesson.body_md: ISH-4404 is a new 4 TB data disk that shows only about 2 TB of usable space after the last technician set it up. A disk's partition table records where each partition starts and ends. The older Master Boot Record format stores those positions as 32-bit sector numbers, so it can address at most 2^32 sectors. With the common 512-byte sectors that is 2,199,023,255,552 bytes, two tebibytes, and anything beyond is simply unreachable. The GUID Partition Table uses 64-bit addresses, supports far larger disks, keeps a backup copy of the table at the end of the disk, and allows many more partitions. A 4,000,000,000,000-byte disk is larger than the MBR ceiling, so it must be GPT. Disks with 4,096-byte native sectors stretch MBR to 16 TiB, but they are not what the bench usually sees. To boot an operating system from a GPT disk, the PC's firmware needs to run in UEFI mode rather than legacy BIOS mode, a setting in the firmware setup screen. Converting the scheme erases the table, so copy the data off and confirm the backup before you touch it.
lesson.worked_example: MBR limit = 2^32 × 512 B = 2,199,023,255,552 B (2 TiB); 4 TB disk > limit → GPT, boot with UEFI; 4096-byte sectors raise the MBR limit to 16 TiB

weeks.title: Fault isolation — symptom first, subsystem second, parts last

lesson.title: Fault isolation — symptom first, subsystem second, parts last
lesson.body_md: ISH-4505 is five machines on the bench at once and a temptation to start swapping motherboards. Good technicians follow the power-on sequence, because each stage that succeeds rules out everything before it. No lights and no fans means the power path: the outlet, the cable, the supply's rear switch, then the supply itself. Fans spinning with beeps and no picture means the board is alive but the self-test failed, most often memory or a processor that is not seated; reseat the sticks one at a time before anything else. A self-test that passes and then complains there is no boot device points at the boot order in the firmware or a disk that is not detected. A machine that boots and then shows a stop error usually blames the last driver or update installed. Random shutdowns only under heavy load suggest heat or an undersized supply, so check temperatures and last week's power budget. Write down the symptom in the customer's words, the stage it fails at, and the cheapest test that would confirm your guess. Replacing parts before isolating the fault costs money and hides the real cause.
lesson.worked_example: T1 fans/no display/beeps → memory_or_cpu_seating; T2 dead → power_path; T3 shuts down under load → thermal_or_psu_capacity; T4 no boot device → boot_order_or_disk; T5 stop error after boot → driver_or_os

weeks.title: Display bandwidth — will the cable carry the mode?

lesson.title: Display bandwidth — will the cable carry the mode?
lesson.body_md: ISH-4606: a donated 4K monitor flickers or drops to 30 Hz on a refurbished PC. A screen mode is a stream of pixels, and the cable has a ceiling. Multiply width by height by refresh rate by bits per pixel: 3,840 by 2,160 at 60 Hz with 24-bit colour is about 11.94 gigabits per second. That ignores the blanking intervals between lines and frames, so the true need is somewhat higher, and the honest label is lower bound. Compare it with each link's usable data rate after encoding overhead: HDMI 1.4 carries about 8.16, HDMI 2.0 about 14.4, and DisplayPort 1.4 about 25.92. The 4K 60 Hz mode fits HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort 1.4 but not HDMI 1.4, which is why the old port falls back to 30 Hz. Double the refresh to 120 Hz and the need becomes about 23.89 Gbit/s, which only DisplayPort 1.4 carries uncompressed here. Cables and ports are both links in the chain: a certified high-speed cable on an old port still runs at the old port's speed, so read both before promising a customer a mode.

weeks.title: UPS runtime — watt-hours, inverter loss, and a graceful shutdown

lesson.title: UPS runtime — watt-hours, inverter loss, and a graceful shutdown
lesson.body_md: ISH-4707: the community centre's storage box and router should ride out short power cuts and shut down cleanly during long ones. A battery's energy is in watt-hours, and the uninterruptible power supply converts it back to mains power through an inverter that loses some energy as heat. This unit holds two 12 V, 36 Ah batteries, about 864 Wh, and its inverter is about 85 percent efficient. The load measured at the wall is 300 W, so the runtime is 864 × 0.85 ÷ 300 hours, about 2.45 hours or 146.9 minutes. Batteries age, cold rooms reduce capacity, and the last minutes of a discharge are not reliable, so the bench starts a graceful shutdown no later than 80 percent of the computed runtime; here the plan picks 110 minutes. Configure the storage box to listen for the UPS's low-battery signal over USB or the network, and test it by pulling the plug while someone watches. Never plug a laser printer or a space heater into the battery outlets; their surges can overload the inverter.
lesson.worked_example: 864 Wh × 0.85 / 300 W × 60 = 146.9 min; start shutdown by 80% → no later than about 117 min (bench picks 110)

weeks.title: Imaging a lab — unicast one by one versus one multicast stream

lesson.title: Imaging a lab — unicast one by one versus one multicast stream
lesson.body_md: ISH-4808: forty refurbished laptops need the same 32 GB system image before the library's coding club opens. Image sizes are in bytes and network links in bits, so start by multiplying by eight: 256 gigabits per copy. On a gigabit link that really delivers about 70 percent of its rating, one copy takes about 366 seconds, a little over six minutes. Sending the image to each laptop separately, unicast, repeats that forty times through the same server port: about 244 minutes, more than four hours. Multicast sends one stream that every listening machine receives together, so in the ideal case the whole lab finishes in about the time of a single copy, roughly six minutes. Real networks need switches that handle multicast properly, and one slow or faulty laptop can hold the session back, so plan a fallback to unicast for stragglers. Whatever the method, check one finished machine against a list of expected settings before releasing the rest, and record which image version went onto which serial numbers.
lesson.worked_example: 32 GB image × 8 = 256 Gbit ÷ (1 Gbit/s × 0.7) = 365.7 s per stream; 40 machines unicast ≈ 243.8 min; multicast ≈ 6.1 min

weeks.title: Media sanitization — Clear, Purge, or Destroy before a device leaves

lesson.title: Media sanitization — Clear, Purge, or Destroy before a device leaves
lesson.body_md: ISH-4909 is the second NO_AI week, because a sanitization decision has to be yours. Donated machines arrive full of strangers' lives, and the bench's promise is that nothing leaves with them. NIST Special Publication 800-88 frames the choice with three words. Clear uses ordinary commands to overwrite user-addressable storage, enough when the device stays inside the organisation. Purge uses methods that defeat laboratory recovery, such as the drive's own secure-erase or cryptographic-erase commands, and is the floor when a device leaves your control through donation, sale, or a returned lease. Destroy means the media cannot be reused: shredding, disintegrating, or incinerating, and it is the only answer for a drive that has failed and will not accept commands. Solid-state drives remap blocks behind the scenes, so overwriting the visible space can leave old data in spare areas; rely on the drive's purge commands. Every decision ends with verification and a certificate recording the serial number, method, date, and who did it. A quick format is none of the three.
lesson.worked_example: RB-1001 HDD reuse_internal → Clear; RB-1002 SSD leave_org → Purge; RB-1003 failed SSD → Destroy; RB-1004 HDD leave_org → Purge; each verified with a certificate ID

weeks.title: Refurb service report — fault, fix, sanitization, proof

lesson.title: Refurb service report — fault, fix, sanitization, proof
lesson.body_md: ISH-4A10 closes the term with the document that travels with each refurbished machine. For every device the report gives the serial number, the fault class from the bench's isolation table, and the fix in plain words, such as reseated the memory stick in A2. It records the sanitization method chosen for the drive and that verification passed, pointing at last week's certificate. It notes anything a new owner should know, like a replacement power supply, the memory mode confirmed in firmware, or a monitor that needs the DisplayPort cable for full refresh. The bench also signs one sentence for the whole batch: no customer data was retained, copied, or looked through beyond what the repair required. Technicians who browse a donor's photos to 'test the drive' end their volunteering that day. Mentors review the report against six or more passed labs, pick one machine at random, and ask the technician to explain the fault and the fix while the case is open. A clean report is what lets a school trust a donated computer.
lesson.worked_example: RB-1002: fault memory_or_cpu_seating, fix reseated DIMM in A2, sanitization Purge, verified; customer_data_retained false
